vtrmc-2011-01.title: Substitute $y=\sqrt x$ and use partial fractions
The substitution $x=4/t$
vtrmc-2011-01.body:
Let $x=\frac4t$, $dx=-\frac4{t^2}dt$; $x=1\leftrightarrow t=4$ and $x=4\leftrightarrow t=1$. Then $x-2=\frac{2(2-t)}{t}$, $x^2+4=\frac{4(4+t^2)}{t^2}$, $\sqrt x=\frac2{\sqrt t}$, and
$$\frac{x-2}{(x^2+4)\sqrt x}\,dx=\frac{2(2-t)}{t}\cdot\frac{t^2}{4(t^2+4)}\cdot\frac{\sqrt t}{2}\cdot\left(-\frac{4}{t^2}\right)dt=\frac{t-2}{(t^2+4)\sqrt t}\,dt .$$
Hence $I=\int_4^1\frac{t-2}{(t^2+4)\sqrt t}\,dt=-I$, so $I=0$.

**Answer: $0$.**

vtrmc-2011-02.title: Guess $a_n=n^2-1$ and prove it by induction

vtrmc-2011-03.title: Telescoping
vtrmc-2011-03.body:
Write $k^2-2=(k+2)(k+1)-3(k+2)+2$. Then
$$\frac{k^2-2}{(k+2)!}=\frac1{k!}-\frac{3}{(k+1)!}+\frac{2}{(k+2)!}=\left(\frac1{k!}-\frac1{(k+1)!}\right)-2\left(\frac1{(k+1)!}-\frac1{(k+2)!}\right).$$
Summing from $k=1$ to $n$, both brackets telescope:
$$S_n=\left(1-\frac1{(n+1)!}\right)-2\left(\frac12-\frac1{(n+2)!}\right)=-\frac1{(n+1)!}+\frac2{(n+2)!}\ \longrightarrow\ 0 .$$

**Answer: $0$.**

vtrmc-2011-03.title: Series for $e$
vtrmc-2011-03.body:
Using the same decomposition $\frac{k^2-2}{(k+2)!}=\frac1{k!}-\frac3{(k+1)!}+\frac2{(k+2)!}$ and $\sum_{j\ge0}\frac1{j!}=e$ (all series converge absolutely):
$$\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{k!}=e-1,\qquad\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{(k+1)!}=e-2,\qquad\sum_{k\ge1}\frac1{(k+2)!}=e-\frac52 .$$
So the sum is $(e-1)-3(e-2)+2\left(e-\frac52\right)=0$.

**Answer: $0$.**

vtrmc-2011-04.title: Subgroup size, then lift $s$ to a unit
vtrmc-2011-04.body:
Let $N=mn$ and $g=\gcd(a,N)$.

**Step 1: $\gcd(a,mn)=n$.** By Bézout, the integers of the form $ar+Nt$ are exactly the multiples of $g$. Hence $\{[ar]\}$ is the set of classes of multiples of $g$, namely $[0],[g],\dots,[N-g]$, which has $N/g$ elements. So $N/g=m$, i.e. $g=n$.

**Step 2.** Thus $n\mid a$; write $a=sn$. Then $n=\gcd(sn,mn)=n\gcd(s,m)$, so $\gcd(s,m)=1$.

**Step 3: find $q\equiv s\pmod m$ prime to $mn$.** Let $t$ be the product of the primes that divide $mn$ but not $s$ ($t=1$ if there are none), and let $q_0=s+tm$. Let $p$ be a prime dividing $mn$.
- If $p\mid s$: then $p\nmid m$ (as $\gcd(s,m)=1$) and $p\nmid t$, so $p\nmid tm$ and $p\nmid s+tm$.
- If $p\nmid s$: then $p\mid t$, so $p\mid tm$ and again $p\nmid s+tm$.

So $\gcd(q_0,mn)=1$. Put $q=q_0+Kmn$ with $K$ large enough that $q>0$; this keeps $q$ prime to $mn$ and $q\equiv s\pmod m$.

**Step 4.** Since $q\equiv s\pmod m$, we get $nq\equiv ns=a\pmod{mn}$, i.e. $[nq]=[a]$. ∎

vtrmc-2011-05.title: Expand the exponential
vtrmc-2011-05.body:
For $y>0$ write $y^{1+1/y}=y\,e^{u}$ with $u=\frac{\ln y}{y}\to0$. Since $e^u=1+u+R(u)$ with $|R(u)|\le u^2$ for $|u|\le1$,
$$y^{1+1/y}=y+\ln y+yR(u),\qquad |yR(u)|\le\frac{(\ln y)^2}{y}\to0 .$$
So $y^{1+1/y}=y+\ln y+o(1)$ as $y\to\infty$. Applying this with $y=2x$ and $y=x$:
$$(2x)^{1+\frac1{2x}}-x^{1+\frac1x}-x=\big(2x+\ln(2x)\big)-\big(x+\ln x\big)-x+o(1)=\ln2+o(1).$$

**Answer: $\ln 2$.**

vtrmc-2011-05.title: L'Hôpital's rule (official approach)
vtrmc-2011-05.body:
Let $f(x)=x^{1+1/x}-x-\ln x$. Then
$$(2x)^{1+\frac1{2x}}-x^{1+\frac1x}-x=f(2x)-f(x)+\ln(2x)-\ln x=f(2x)-f(x)+\ln2,$$
so it suffices to show $f(x)\to0$.

Write $f(x)=x\,g(x)$ with $g(x)=x^{1/x}-1-\frac{\ln x}{x}$. Since $\ln x^{1/x}=\frac{\ln x}x\to0$, $g(x)\to0$, so $f(x)=\frac{g(x)}{1/x}$ is a $\frac00$ form. With $\left(x^{1/x}\right)'=x^{1/x}\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$ and $\left(\frac{\ln x}x\right)'=\frac{1-\ln x}{x^2}$,
$$\frac{g'(x)}{-1/x^2}=-x^2\cdot\frac{(1-\ln x)\left(x^{1/x}-1\right)}{x^2}=(\ln x-1)\left(x^{1/x}-1\right).$$
Finally $x^{1/x}-1=e^{u}-1$ with $u=\frac{\ln x}x$, and $0\le e^u-1\le 2u$ for small $u\ge0$, so $0\le(\ln x-1)(x^{1/x}-1)\le\frac{2(\ln x)^2}{x}\to0$ (for large $x$). By L'Hôpital, $f(x)\to0$, and the limit is $\ln 2$.

**Answer: $\ln 2$.**

vtrmc-2011-06.title: Lexicographic product with the rationals
vtrmc-2011-06.body:
Note first that an asymmetric relation is irreflexive: $a<a$ would imply "not $a<a$".

**Construction.** Let $T_0=S\times\mathbb Q$ with
$$(a,p)\prec(b,q)\iff a<b,\ \text{ or }\ a=b\text{ and }p<q .$$
Identify each $s\in S$ with $(s,0)$; formally, let $T$ be $S$ together with the elements $(s,p)$, $p\ne0$, where $s\in S$ stands for $(s,0)$, and transport $\prec$ along this bijection with $T_0$. So $T\supseteq S$.

**$\prec$ is asymmetric.** Suppose $(a,p)\prec(b,q)$ and $(b,q)\prec(a,p)$.
- If $a<b$, the second relation needs $b<a$ (impossible by asymmetry) or $b=a$ (then $a<a$, impossible).
- If $a=b$ and $p<q$, the second relation needs $a<a$ (impossible) or $q<p$ (impossible).

**$\prec$ extends $<$.** For $a,b\in S$: $(a,0)\prec(b,0)$ iff $a<b$ or ($a=b$ and $0<0$), i.e. iff $a<b$.

**Density.** Let $(a,p)\prec(b,q)$.
- If $a<b$: take $t=(a,p+1)$. Then $(a,p)\prec t$ (same first coordinate, $p<p+1$) and $t\prec(b,q)$ (as $a<b$).
- If $a=b$ and $p<q$: take $t=\left(a,\frac{p+q}2\right)$; then $(a,p)\prec t\prec(a,q)$.

Hence $T$ has all the required properties. ∎

vtrmc-2011-07.title: Vieta and Cauchy–Schwarz
vtrmc-2011-07.body:
Suppose all $100$ roots $x_1,\dots,x_{100}$ (with multiplicity) are real. By Vieta's formulas,
$$\sum x_i=-20,\qquad\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j=198,\qquad\prod x_i=(-1)^{100}\cdot1=1 .$$
Hence
$$\sum x_i^2=\Big(\sum x_i\Big)^2-2\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j=400-396=4 .$$
By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality with the vector $(1,\dots,1)$,
$$400=\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{100}x_i\Big)^2\le100\sum_{i=1}^{100}x_i^2=400,$$
so equality holds, which forces $(x_1,\dots,x_{100})$ to be a multiple of $(1,\dots,1)$: all $x_i$ are equal, hence $x_i=-\frac{20}{100}=-\frac15$. But then $\prod x_i=5^{-100}\neq1$, a contradiction.

So $P$ has a non-real root. ∎

vtrmc-2011-07.title: Variance
vtrmc-2011-07.body: For real roots, the mean is $\mu=\frac{-20}{100}=-\frac15$ and the mean square is $\frac{4}{100}=\frac1{25}$ (computed as above from Vieta). The variance $\frac1{100}\sum(x_i-\mu)^2=\frac1{25}-\mu^2=0$, so every $x_i=-\frac15$ and $P(x)=\left(x+\frac15\right)^{100}$, whose constant term $5^{-100}$ is not $1$. Contradiction, so some root is non-real. ∎
